title: the Rudram
hook: the Rudram bows to the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest, and even the middle child

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rudram gave us its heartbeat, namah, a bow said again and again. Did a hello become a small bow? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.
screen: `NAMAH — A BOW.` · `TODAY: WHO GETS THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Some family photos have a pecking order. The eldest stands in the middle, the youngest gets pulled onto someone's lap, and the middle one is somewhere near the edge, half out of frame. A photo like that has its rankings, spoken or not. Partway through the Rudram, the hymn walks right into that photo. It bows to the eldest. It bows to the youngest. And then it does something families don't always do. It bows to the middle one too.
screen: `A FAMILY PHOTO.` → `THE MIDDLE ONE, HALF OUT OF FRAME.` → `THE HYMN BOWS TO ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: In one stretch of the Namakam, the bows come in pairs. A bow to the short one, and to the dwarf. A bow to the large one, and to the one grown old. A bow to the eldest, and to the youngest. A bow to the firstborn, and to the one born after. A bow to the middle one, and to the one not yet grown, still young and unsure. Rudra is all of them. Hear what that does. Short and tall, old and young, first and last: these are the measures people can use to rank each other. Who's bigger. Who came first. Who's the grown-up. The hymn doesn't erase the differences. It names every one. But it bows to every one, with the same small word, the same weight. Nobody's namah is louder. The eldest doesn't get a longer line. That fits what the Rudram has been doing all along. Last week it found Rudra in the sun that cowherds see. Here it finds him in the whole family, down to the one who hasn't figured themselves out yet. There's a gentleness hiding in that last pair. The Sanskrit word there points to someone not yet bold, not yet sure of themselves. A hymn to a fierce god stops to bow to the shy one. On the hymn's terms, if Rudra is the youngest and the eldest, then the kid at the end of the table is no less holy than the grandparent at the head. In this hymn, the bow doesn't go up the ladder. It goes to every rung.
screen: `THE SHORT AND THE TALL.` · `THE ELDEST AND THE YOUNGEST.` · `THE MIDDLE ONE, AND THE SHY ONE.` · `THE SAME BOW FOR EVERY RUNG.` · then, large: `NOBODY'S NAMAH IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow down the family line. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the people in your family, or the family you've made, in order. The eldest you can think of. Then the next. Then on down, to the youngest. Spend a breath with each, and give each the same inward bow. Notice if one is harder to bow to. Stay a little longer with that one. If you pray, you can say namah for each of them. The bell holds the time.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the eldest and the youngest, the firstborn and the later-born, the middle one and the shy one.
Your line: the Rudram. Today, in any group you're part of, notice who's in the middle or at the edge, and give them your full attention once. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Chanters learn the Namakam's paired lines (namo jyeshthaya cha kanishthaya cha and others) by heart, usually from a teacher, and recite them in Vedic Sanskrit at home, in temples and in group chanting.
